lesson.title: ist, war & bin: Being Cognates
lesson.subtitle: The sein paradigm via cognates — and war/was drills closing the Perfekt loop

hook.title: The Fossil Bed
hook.content: The sein paradigm is three ancient verbs in a trench coat: *es- gives ist and sind; *bʰu- gives bin and bist; *wes- gives war and gewesen. English wears the same coat: is/are from *es-, be/am from *bʰu-, was/been from *wes-. ist ↔ is is letter-for-letter. war ↔ was is one letter apart. gewesen ↔ been — both the participle of the *wes- root. Today: drill the paradigm through its twins, and close the Perfekt loop — sein is not just the motion auxiliary from topic 18, it is the word war you need for storytelling.

footnotes.title: The Simple Past Returns
footnotes.content: Perfekt replaced the spoken simple past for most verbs — but sein and haben keep their simple pasts in daily speech: ich war, ich hatte. 'ich bin gewesen' exists but is far rarer than 'ich war' for 'I was'. The two most common verbs are the fortress where the old past tense survives.

pattern.title: The Paradigm, Twin by Twin
pattern.content: ich bin ↔ I am / I be. du bist ↔ thou art. er ist ↔ he is (letter for letter). wir sind ↔ we are (different branch, same verb). sie sind ↔ they are. And the past: ich war ↔ I was, du warst ↔ thou wast, er war ↔ he was. The Perfekt loop closes: Ich bin gewesen ↔ I have been; Ich bin gestern nach Berlin gefahren — sein doing motion duty. Sentence pattern for storytelling: Gestern war gut. Das Haus war alt. Der Kaffee war gut. war is the storyteller's tense for the copula — drill it until war/was feels like one word, because it is.
pattern.linguist_note: bist ↔ art is the oldest 2nd-person singular in either language — thou art and du bist are the same construction, with the -st ending you have drilled since the Shakespeare lesson and the b-root of 'be'.

exercises.prompt: The paradigm wall — match each sein-form with its twin:
exercises.target_answer: ist, war, du bist, gewesen, ich bin ein Mensch
exercises.meaning: is, was, thou art, been, I am a person
exercises.explanation: Three roots, one verb, identical across the sea — the most conservative words in Germanic. der Mensch (human — the mannish kin) takes sein like any noun: der Mensch ist alt.

exercises.prompt: Storytelling check: 'Gestern _____ alles gut.' (Yesterday everything WAS good):
exercises.meaning: Gestern war alles gut = Yesterday everything was good
exercises.explanation: sein keeps its simple past in speech: war. The storyteller's tense — and war ↔ was, one letter apart. Die Leute (the people) tell it: Der Himmel war blau — every story opens with war.

exercises.meaning: Du bist alt = you are old (thou art old)
exercises.explanation: du bist ↔ thou art — the *bʰu- root wearing the -st you drilled in the Thou -st Circuit. The being-idioms: ich bin krank, satt, glücklich — ich habe Hunger — sein carries the feelings, haben carries the hunger.

exercises.prompt: Close the Perfekt loop: which sentence uses sein for MOTION?
exercises.meaning: sein for motion, haben for objects — the loop closes
exercises.explanation: The topic-18 choice gym, now with the sein paradigm fully in hand: motion → bin/ist/ist gefahren. holen is haben's — Wir haben wieder Brot geholt — fetch again, haben again.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'Yesterday was cold but today is good'
exercises.target_answer: Gestern war kalt aber heute ist gut
exercises.meaning: Yesterday was cold but today is good

vocab_hints.note: no English twin — just the oldest coordinating word in the German toolbox

exercises.explanation: war and ist in one sentence — the *wes- past and the *es- present, both twins, both daily.

summary.outcome: Conjugate sein through its cognate twins and tell yesterday's story with war.

use_example.german: Gestern war kalt, aber heute ist gut.
use_example.english: Yesterday was cold, but today is good.

summary.takeaway: ist↔is, war↔was, bist↔art — three roots shared across the sea, and war is the storyteller's tense.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Wie geht's? — the greetings and small-talk idioms as archaic English survivals.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from ist, war & bin: Being Cognates (Yesterday was cold but today is good):
twist.target_answer: Gestern war kalt aber heute ist gut
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Gestern war kalt aber heute ist gut" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of ist, war & bin: Being Cognates without relying on short-term echo.

morgen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English morrow (hence to-morrow) and morn — both descend from the Germanic root for "morning". [wiktionary]

leute.context_translation: Many people are waiting at the station.
leute.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *liudiz, kin to the Old English leode (men, people); German keeps the plural-only collective with the standard article die Leute. [wiktionary]

himmel.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *himil — the same Germanic line as English heaven's root family. [wiktionary]

mensch.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *manniskaz 'human', built on Mann — English mannish is the cognate form. [wiktionary]

hunger.context_translation: I have great hunger / I am very hungry.

krank.context_phrase: Ich bin krank und bleibe zu Hause.
krank.context_translation: I am sick and staying home.
krank.etymology_derivation: Old sense 'crooked, weak' — Wiktionary: cognate with English crank. [wiktionary]

satt.etymology_derivation: From Old High German sat, Proto-Germanic *sadaz, meaning sated or full; the exact cognate is English sad, which originally meant sated before it drifted to its modern sorrowful sense. [wiktionary]

glücklich.etymology_derivation: Glück (luck) + -lich; Wiktionary: 'Compare English luck' — a relative via Dutch. [wiktionary]

holen.context_phrase: Ich hole Wasser aus der Küche.
holen.context_translation: I am getting water from the kitchen.
holen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *holōną (to fetch); the page documents cognate English haul — the same hauling-and-fetching word. [wiktionary]

wieder.context_translation: We will see each other again.
wieder.etymology_derivation: Old High German widar 'against', from West Germanic *wiþr 'toward, against' — the page names English wither and widdershins as cognates; German wieder turned against into again. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
